title: The Brutal History of Prison Labor
summary: Josh and Chuck trace the history of prison labor in the United States, from English transportation of convicts to the colonies and the Thomas More "Utopia" idea of work as punishment, through the Thirteenth Amendment loophole, convict leasing in the post-Civil War South, chain gangs, the Parchman Farm trustee system, the 1970-2008 mass incarceration boom, and modern prison wages, private-industry work, UNICOR, and reform debates. The episode also includes a sponsor read for Cooperative for Education (CoEd) and a listener mail segment from Kimberly suggesting an episode on crowds.
topics: I Am a Fugitive from a Georgia Chain Gang

segments.title: Cooperative for Education sponsor read (opening)
segments.summary: Sponsor read asking listeners to support Cooperative for Education's RISE Youth Development program in Guatemala.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on prison labor, with Jerry on leave, and tease the historical arc.

segments.title: Thomas More's Utopia and the benefits of prison labor
segments.summary: Chuck explains that before the 16th century punishments were lethal or corporal, and Thomas More's Utopia proposed putting offenders to work. Josh outlines the three goals: deterrence, rehabilitation, and free labor.

segments.title: Transportation of convicts to the colonies
segments.summary: British convicts were transported to the American colonies, known as King's passengers, and colonial plantation owners and employers saw them as cheap labor, compared with the cost of enslaved Africans.

segments.title: Indentured servitude and plantation punishment
segments.summary: Chuck explains that indentured servitude applied to white people in the colonies, and that plantation owners were left to punish enslaved people without state intervention. Hosts briefly discuss the film 12 Years a Slave.

segments.title: Transported convicts' fate in America
segments.summary: Hosts describe that about ninety percent of transported convicts went to Maryland and Virginia to work in industry or tobacco farming, serving terms of seven to fourteen years.

segments.title: Origins of the penitentiary and Auburn model
segments.summary: Chuck explains jails versus penitentiaries, with Quakers credited with the penitentiary idea. Josh notes penitent root and redemptive suffering. Auburn Prison in New York is described as a model where private businesses leased prison buildings and prisoners; Auburn prisoners built Sing Sing.

segments.title: Northern model and the Thirteenth Amendment loophole
segments.summary: By the Civil War, the Northern model let businesses rent prisoners. The South stayed tied to chattel slavery. The Thirteenth Amendment abolished involuntary servitude except as punishment for crime, a loophole that enabled prison labor. Chuck mentions the documentary 13th.

segments.title: Black Codes and pretextual arrests
segments.summary: Southern Black Codes criminalized being a free Black person, with vagrancy arrests leading to leasing out to plantation owners. Hosts reference an earlier episode on the Black Codes and note the Civil Rights Act of 1866 and Fourteenth Amendment.

segments.title: Convict leasing in Georgia, Alabama and other states
segments.summary: Georgia's provisional governor Thomas Ruger leased prisoners in 1868, including 100 Black prisoners to William Fort of the Georgia and Alabama Railroad for $25 each; sixteen died in the first year. Convict leasing grew, reaching 73 percent of Alabama state revenue by 1898. Chuck notes prisoner deaths in custody remain unaccountable today.

segments.title: Southern convict leasing conditions and corporate use
segments.summary: Northern prison labor was eight to nine hours a day, while Southern work often ran twelve to sixteen hours. Pretextual arrests before cotton harvests are described. Sloss Sheffield Steel and Iron Company had a ten percent death rate; Texas leased prisoners to Imperial Sugar in Sugarland, Tennessee, where many died of malaria. Louisiana's New Orleans railway used prison labor with about 140 deaths.

segments.title: Legacy of leasing, New Deal and UNICOR
segments.summary: Chuck notes that convicts' goods still reach consumers today. Hosts discuss that the New Deal era ended interstate sale of prison-made goods and that Federal Prison Industries (now UNICOR) was created in 1934. Question raised about private federal prisons.

segments.title: UNICOR procurement and private prison criticism
segments.summary: Hosts note that UNICOR products and government procurement rules draw complaints about unfair competition. They say a future episode on private prisons is needed.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Mid-episode ad break.

segments.title: Parchman Farm and the trustee system
segments.summary: After convict leasing waned in the North due to unions, Southern states shifted to state-owned farms. Parchman Farm in Mississippi, a 20,000-acre farm with a roughly 90 percent Black prison population in the early 1910s, used armed trustees to supervise other prisoners.

segments.title: Chain gangs and road building
segments.summary: Hosts describe chain gangs in the South in the 1920s building roads, chained at the ankle, with abuse; a Tucker Farm in Arkansas investigation found torture at the prison hospital. Women prisoners also did field work.

segments.title: Chain gang labor, Toni Morrison and racial framework
segments.summary: Chuck describes manual road building without machinery, with sledgehammers used on rock. Josh notes the racist framework of chain gangs, including white labor camps. Chuck says the threat of chain gangs pushed Black workers into poorly paid jobs.

segments.title: Chain gang exposure and their decline
segments.summary: Robert Burns's 1932 book I Am a Fugitive from a Georgia Chain Gang and its film adaptation publicized conditions. Bayard Rustin wrote articles for the New York Post in 1947 after being held on a North Carolina chain gang. Chain gangs faded in the 1950s and 1960s; Sheriff Joe Arpaio of Maricopa County pushed to revive them but it did not happen.

segments.title: Mid-episode break transition
segments.summary: Short break before the modern era section.

segments.title: Mass incarceration from 1970 to 2008
segments.summary: Incarcerated population rose about 700 percent from 1970 to 2008 while the US population rose about 50 percent. Hosts credit Nixon's war on drugs, Reagan's tough-on-crime stance, and Clinton policies. Imprisonment peaked in 2008 at about 1.6 million, then fell to about 1.3 million. The US incarceration rate is compared with El Salvador's gang crackdown.

segments.title: Modern prison work and license plates
segments.summary: About 800,000 people in state and federal prison work, roughly 80 percent for the prison itself. Around 2 percent of federal prison workers work for UNICOR. Utah's license plate operation (Plate Busters) and New Hampshire's Live Free or Die plates are discussed.

segments.title: Dangerous prison jobs and private industry work
segments.summary: California prisoners fight wildfires for about two to five dollars a day plus one dollar an hour. About 40,000 incarcerated workers, around 5 percent, work for private industry, sometimes in fast food or hotel custodial work. Corporate policies against prison labor are hard to enforce through supply chains and franchises.

segments.title: Prison wages, deductions and conditions
segments.summary: There is no federal law requiring pay for prisoners. The average prison wage is about 52 cents an hour, with deductions for room and board and victim restitution. Hosts describe a women's prison in Georgia where food is so poor that prisoners dig through guards' trash, citing a writer named Carla Simmons.

segments.title: Reform proposals and lack of worker protections
segments.summary: Reformers want prison labor to build job skills, fair federal minimum wage, and worker protections. Courts have ruled prisoners are not employees under OSHA or the Fair Labor Standards Act. A 2024 Alabama lawsuit was dismissed, with the state calling the work mandatory chores.

segments.title: International forced labor standards
segments.summary: Walk Free's Global Slavery Index lists the US among countries using state-imposed forced labor. The US has not ratified the 1930 Forced Labor Convention, and the Senate declined in 1991 partly because of conflicts with private subcontracting.

segments.title: State constitutional bans and Nebraska economic study
segments.summary: Seven states, including Alabama and Tennessee, have constitutional bans on forced prison labor, requiring pay and banning coercive punishments. An Edgeworth Economics Group study found Nebraska's prison work produces about $15 billion a year in savings and that paying prisoner wages would yield two to three dollars in societal return per dollar.

segments.title: Listener mail from Kimberly: crowds and line etiquette
segments.summary: Kimberly suggests an episode on how people move through crowds and avoid crowd crushes. Hosts share airport boarding line anecdotes and credit her for the idea.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts explain how to send listener mail to Stuff Podcasts at iHeartRadio dot com and close the episode.
